## [Homepage](../index.html)

These exercises accompany Units [K](../un_K.html) and [L](../un_L.html).

The exercises whose title carries a number such as [(**AK** 6.15)]{.grey} are
taken, sometimes in a simplified form, from @Agresti2022; their data are those
of the [website of the book](https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/).

The [solution]{.blue} of each exercise is in a separate **R** script, linked
from the title of the exercise itself.

## Simple linear regression

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### `forbes` dataset - Solution: [`forbes.R`](../code/forbes.R)

Let us go back to the `forbes` data of [Unit F](../un_F.html): the boiling
temperature of water and the atmospheric pressure at $17$ locations in the
Alps. As in Unit F, convert the temperature into degrees Celsius.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Fit the simple linear regression model with response `Pressure` and
    explanatory variable `TempC` using `lm`. Check that the estimates are those
    obtained in Unit F, and interpret the slope.

2.  Is the temperature related to the pressure? Test $H_0: \beta = 0$ and
    compute the $95\%$ confidence interval for $\beta$.

3.  Water boils at $97$ degrees Celsius. Compute the confidence interval for
    the mean pressure and the prediction interval for the pressure at that
    location. Which one is wider, and why?

4.  Plot the residuals against the fitted values. Is there any location with a
    much larger residual than the others?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### `Houses` dataset [(**AK** 6.15)]{.grey} - Solution: [`Houses_lm.R`](../code/Houses_lm.R)

The `Houses` data of [Exercises B](exe_B.html) are available at [this
link](https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Houses.dat). Consider the selling
price (`price`, thousands of dollars), the size (`size`, square feet) and the
annual tax bill (`taxes`, dollars).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Fit the model with response `price` and explanatory variable `size`.
    Interpret the slope and its $95\%$ confidence interval.

2.  Compute the confidence interval for the mean price of the houses of
    $2000$ square feet, and the prediction interval for the price of a single
    house of $2000$ square feet.

3.  Add `taxes` to the model. How does the effect of `size` change? Why?
    [Hint]{.blue}: compute the correlation between `size` and `taxes`.
:::

## Multiple linear regression

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### `UN` dataset [(adapted from **AK** 6.12)]{.grey} - Solution: [`UN_lm.R`](../code/UN_lm.R)

The `UN` data of [Exercises B](exe_B.html) are available at [this
link](https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/UN.dat). Consider the carbon dioxide
emissions per capita (`CO2`, metric tons), the per capita gross domestic
product (`GDP`, thousands of dollars) and the percentage of people using the
Internet (`Internet`).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Fit the model with response `CO2` and explanatory variable `GDP`. Is the
    effect of `GDP` statistically significant?

2.  Add `Internet` to the model. Are the two variables statistically
    significant? What does the F test in the last line of `summary` say?

3.  The results of point 2 may look contradictory. [Hint]{.blue}: compute the
    correlation between `GDP` and `Internet`, and recall that each $t$ test
    asks whether a variable is useful [given the other one]{.orange}.

4.  Compare the values of $R^2$ of the two models. Does `Internet` improve the
    fit appreciably?
:::
